content.overview: Post-dry quality continues to change. Light, oxygen, temperature, humidity, package permeability, time and product matrix influence cannabinoid and volatile stability, so storage should be treated as a controlled condition rather than passive shelf time.

vocabulary.definition: Gas volume within a sealed package above or around the product.
A package material's resistance to transfer of gases, moisture or light.
The degree to which defined product attributes remain within acceptable change over time.

sections.title: Storage changes chemistry over time
sections.body: Research across cannabis matrices consistently identifies time, temperature, light and oxygen as stability variables, though the magnitude differs by product type and condition.

sections.title: Packaging effects are empirical, not magical
sections.body: A 2024 modified-atmosphere study found nitrogen packaging influenced some individual compounds but did not universally preserve total cannabinoids and aromatics, illustrating why packaging claims require measured validation.

sections.title: Curing can change moisture condition
sections.body: A 2025 hemp study observed moisture changes during cure, reinforcing the need to measure product condition rather than assuming sealed storage means stability.

workedExamples: If a package reduces oxygen exposure but allows moisture exchange, chemical and microbial stability questions remain separate.
A storage technology that preserves one terpene may not improve total volatile retention.
commonMistakes: Assuming airtight means stable under every temperature and light condition.
Treating packaging marketing claims as validation data.
Ignoring storage duration when comparing lab results.
content.practicalApplication: Define storage conditions by container, closure, light exposure, temperature, humidity where relevant, lot date and sampling intervals; compare measured change over time.
content.summary: Storage quality is controlled by the interaction of product, package, environment and time.
